claims.text: A hybrid machine-learning model can predict the conductivity of bulk HfNbTaTiZr containing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen across 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
The hybrid model will be significantly more accurate than conventional analytical models.
Conventional analytical conductivity models assume perfect, defect-free crystals.
The investigated material is bulk equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr containing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
The HfNbTaTiZr specimens are produced by additive manufacturing.
Additive manufacturing inherently introduces grain-related defects and oxygen interstitials into these specimens.
The proposed framework couples defect-aware electronic transport theory with high-throughput conductivity measurements spanning the target temperatures.
Defect density and grain size are model inputs.
Using specimens with similar processing histories will ensure consistent defect profiles.
Oxygen-induced defects, dislocations, and grain-boundary characteristics mediate electron and phonon scattering.
The resulting scattering changes the alloy's conduction properties.
Integrating measured conductivity data and oxygen/defect descriptors enables the model to capture scattering mechanisms omitted from ideal-crystal models.
Explicitly parameterizing real microstructural imperfections reduces conductivity-prediction error.
The model will predict held-out conductivity at 250 K within 10% of the measured value.
The model will outperform analytical approaches that omit defect effects.
Traditional analytical models usually have larger discrepancies for oxygen-doped specimens.
Applicability is limited to additively manufactured bulk HfNbTaTiZr containing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen and to 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
Predictions outside the stated temperature windows or at substantially different oxygen contents may be unreliable.
Error reduction may vary because of uncharacterized defect states, extreme-temperature effects, and spatial variation in oxygen.
A deviation greater than 10% between the 250 K prediction and a measurement on a newly fabricated specimen falsifies the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The held-out benchmark is 250 K, but 250 K lies in the excluded 200–300 K gap and therefore outside the model's stated validation and applicability windows. The decisive falsification test consequently evaluates the model where the hypothesis says its predictions are not validated.

The intervention and training design describe measurements across the continuous 0–1200 K interval, whereas the conditions and boundary restrict measurements and validation to the disjoint 0–200 K and 300–1200 K windows.
